tldr: The paper proposes PIT (ImPlicit Self-ImprovemenT), a framework that enables LLMs to implicitly learn self-improvement goals from human preference data by reformulating RLHF to maximize the quality gap between improved and reference responses, eliminating the need for manual rubric design.
contributions: Introducing PIT, a framework that learns self-improvement implicitly from preference data without requiring explicit rubric design
Reformulating RLHF training objectives to maximize response quality gap conditioned on reference responses instead of absolute response quality
Proposing curriculum reinforcement learning with multiple rounds to progressively improve PIT by using reference responses sampled from increasingly better models

Demonstrating through experiments on two real-world datasets (Anthropic/HH-RLHF helpful subset with 161K pairs, OpenAI/Summary with 92.9K training data) and one synthetic dataset (13K examples from PaLM 2) that PIT significantly outperforms prompting-based methods like Self-Refine
methods: PIT is trained in three stages following RLHF: (1) Supervised fine-tuning where PIT maximizes the likelihood of better responses y_w given input x and worse reference y_l, using loss L_SFT_PIT = -log M_PIT(y_w|x, y_l). (2) Reward model training where R_PIT learns to predict quality gaps r_gap(x, y_1, y_2) using a pairwise loss over all response pairs. (3) Curriculum reinforcement learning in two rounds: first optimizing with reference responses from annotated data (y_l, y_w), then sampling reference responses from the policy model M_RL_P for further improvement. At inference, PIT generates improved responses y_1 ~ M_PIT(·|x, y_ref) where y_ref is sampled from the policy model, and the process can be repeated iteratively. The authors used PaLM 2 (Bison) as the backbone model trained on TPU v4.
results: PIT significantly outperforms prompting-based methods (Self-Refine) across all three datasets. The method successfully improved response quality as measured by both GPT-4 evaluations and DeBERTa-Large reward model evaluations. For evaluation, GPT-4 was used on 128 examples and DeBERTa-Large on 1,000 examples per dataset. The reward distribution from R_PIT on the synthetic dataset followed the expected pattern from the loss design (Equation 1), with negative rewards observed when two responses were identical, indicating PIT penalizes repeating reference responses.
limitations: The first round of curriculum reinforcement learning (Optimization_RL,0_PIT) is necessary; removing it and directly optimizing the second round causes PIT to fail to improve policy model responses
Purely training PIT only on the first round also fails since PIT never sees data sampled from the policy model
The method was only evaluated using GPT-4, DeBERTa-Large, and its own reward model as evaluators, which may introduce evaluator-specific biases
Only the helpful subset of HH-RLHF was used; the harmless subset was not experimented with
Unlikelihood loss was found to cause performance degradation during SFT and was therefore excluded
